messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Darius had been nine years old when his uncle’s boot shattered the dining table, followed by the wet crack of his mother’s shoulder against the wall. He remembered the metallic taste of his fear and the absolute stillness that fell when the police finally dragged him out, a silence that now made every sudden noise in his own home feel like a precursor to catastrophe. Because Darius had come to believe the world operated on hidden cruelties and that his childhood passivity was an unforgivable moral failure, he found it impossible to believe anyone when they promised the violence would not return. His internal conviction that he was fundamentally compromised directly fueled his constant state of physical readiness; he began waking before dawn, convinced danger was always circling just outside his awareness. That relentless state of dread quickly pushed him into habits that kept him functioning but never allowed him to rest. He could no longer tolerate quiet rooms, so he made sure never to be alone with another person, constantly moving between the tractor cab and the equipment shed to stay within sight of other laborers. When memories of his mother’s bruised face surfaced during the afternoon heat, he tried hard not to think about the trauma, pressing his palms against his steering wheel until the image dissolved into static. Yet the suppression never truly worked; instead, the unprocessed anger curdled into a quiet obsession with revenge, a mental ledger he kept of every hypothetical way to make the past pay. His refusal to feel safe and his constant scanning of the field perimeters meant that even his partner’s steady voice telling him he was safe now felt like a lie, which deepened his conviction that life was fundamentally broken. The strategies he deployed to survive the aftermath ultimately deepened the very wounds they were meant to cover. By constantly checking on his partner and refusing to let her drive past a neighbor’s house without him, he convinced himself he was irreparably broken. His avoidance and suppression fed a crushing sense of misery; he used to be a happy person who laughed at church potlucks, but the more he policed his reactions, the more he lost his faith in people, life, or a higher power. He became certain he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and that conviction hardened into a permanent posture of guilt. Because he could not trust that the danger had passed, he remained locked in a cycle where his own avoidance only validated his negative beliefs, and those beliefs only amplified his threat response. Every time he avoided the quiet of his bedroom or redirected his attention to fantasies of retribution, his body stayed in a state of permanent alert, ensuring that a distant shout or a slamming car door would instantly trigger the same suffocating dread. By the third year of their relationship, the consequences of that tightening loop became concrete. He missed two harvest shifts because he paced the irrigation ditches waiting for coworkers, and his fiancée eventually moved to the guest house, exhausted by his constant need for her to stay within arm’s reach during storms. That visceral collapse, paired with the loss of his fiancée, is what finally brought him to the clinic. He sits in the intake chair now with his shoulders rigid, most afraid that the fear will never let him rest, but quietly hoping someone might help him believe he can finally lay down his guard.
